clue.text: Invite round for report on high-level activities

parts.note: to court someone is to woo or invite their attention
round in shape, like a circle

explanation.surface: Someone sends out invitations to a round of reports on what senior people are up to.
explanation.walkthrough: The Court Circular is the daily published record of the British royal family's official engagements.
explanation.definitionFit: The Court Circular is a newspaper record of royal engagements, the highest-level social activities in Britain.

clue.text: No straight talking in this Dickensian office

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the obstructive government department in Little Dorrit

explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Little Dorrit, the Circumlocution Office is a satire of bureaucracy whose skill is 'how not to do it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Circumlocution means using many words evasively, and Dickens named his useless government department after it.

clue.text: Tight nut that's becoming loose

definitions.note: used as a verb: to set free

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, and drunk words stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
i.e., id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A nut screwed on tight is working itself loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' looks like it describes the nut, but it means drunk and signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a knot or a captive is to undo or release it, which is what untie means.

clue.text: Riding? Do get a form of insurance

parts.note: Yorkshire was historically split into three Ridings, the word coming from Old Norse for a third part
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A horse rider asks whether a party should take out insurance.
explanation.walkthrough: A riding was one of the three divisions of the old English county of Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Third-party insurance is the minimum cover in Britain, paying out only for damage done to others.

clue.text: Patient having expired?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sick person, stressed on the first syllable
second meaning: no longer valid, like an old passport, stressed on the second syllable

explanation.walkthrough: The question suggests a patient who has died; expired means only out of date.
explanation.definitionFit: An invalid is a person disabled by illness, and an expired ticket is no longer legally valid.

clue.text: Stopping a bottleneck? Super!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: pushing a stopper into a bottle's neck
second meaning: old-fashioned British slang for excellent

explanation.walkthrough: A bottleneck usually means a traffic jam; here it is the literal neck of a bottle. Corking is dated British slang for splendid.
explanation.definitionFit: Corking a bottle seals its neck with a cork, and 'corking' is a chirpy British word for marvellous.

clue.text: Bill — tip, too

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an itemised roll or catalogue, as a bill of fare
second meaning: to lean or heel over, as a ship does

explanation.walkthrough: Bill and tip together suggest paying at a restaurant; each is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a written itemised record, and a ship that tips to one side is said to heel or lean.

clue.text: Having trouble with joints in space over loft, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the words are taken by their sound rather than their spelling

parts.note: room means space
an attic is a loft

explanation.surface: Someone with aching joints has trouble in the room below the loft.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheumatic describes someone afflicted with rheumatism, which causes stiff and painful joints.

clue.text: Make wasted effort to sell an obsolete narcotic

parts.note: flog is British slang for sell
an and a are the same article
dead means no longer in use
horse is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A dealer tries to sell a drug that nobody wants any more.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog a dead horse is an idiom for persisting with a hopeless cause or effort.

clue.text: Briefly have terrier changed for another dog

indicators.note: something changed has been altered, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the contracted form of have, as in I've
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone swaps their terrier for a different breed of dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The terrier is fodder, not the dog defined; 'another dog' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A retriever is a gun-dog breed, so it is a different kind of canine from the terrier.

clue.text: Mean to be charming

definitions.note: the noun spell, a charm, is what 'charming' points to
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an enchantment or charm cast by a witch

explanation.surface: Someone sets out with the intention of being delightful company.
explanation.walkthrough: Mean looks like an adjective (unkind) or a verb of intention; it is the verb signify.
explanation.definitionFit: To spell trouble is to signify it, and a spell is a magic charm cast on someone.

clue.text: Having gained purpose, give a tip

parts.note: up as in 'ten pounds up': ahead, having gained
an end is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: Someone who has found a purpose in life offers a piece of advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' suggests advice or a gratuity; here it is to tip over.
explanation.definitionFit: To upend something is to tip it over so it stands on its end or upside down.

clue.text: Prepared an about-face

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word that follows is read the other way

parts.note: a dial is the face of a clock or watch; dial is also slang for a person's face

explanation.surface: Someone got ready for a complete change of position.
explanation.walkthrough: About-face reads as a single word for a U-turn, but 'about' acts on 'face' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A laid table or laid plans are ones set out and made ready in advance.

clue.text: Air pollution finally kills cat

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word it qualifies, keeping only its closing letter

parts.note: the closing letter of kills
mog, or moggy, is British slang for a cat

explanation.surface: Polluted air in the end proves deadly to a pet cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Smog is a thick blend of smoke and fog that hangs over cities as air pollution.

clue.text: Drift thus from Eton or Oxford to the City?

definitions.text: Drift thus from Eton or Oxford to the City?

parts.words: Drift thus from Eton or Oxford to the City?
parts.note: surface reading: the familiar career slide of public-school and Oxbridge graduates into banking

parts.words: Drift thus from Eton or Oxford to the City?
parts.note: setter's reading: all three sit on the Thames, so floating from either to London follows the current

explanation.walkthrough: Eton, Oxford and the City of London are all on the River Thames, Oxford and Eton upriver of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving with the river's flow from an upriver town toward London is travelling in the direction the water runs.

clue.text: Boy holding map showing frozen north

indicators.note: holding means grasping, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: a lad is a boy
a plan is a map or drawing of a place

explanation.surface: A boy clutches a map of the Arctic wastes.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapland is the Arctic region of northern Scandinavia and Finland, a byword for snowbound far north.

clue.text: Left a piece of paper in office

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
a folio is a single leaf of paper

explanation.surface: Someone has left a sheet of paper behind at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' looks like a workplace but means a ministerial post.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister's portfolio is the area of government responsibility attached to their post or office.

clue.text: Downfall of the Gods not by supposed author

indicators.note: a downfall is a collapse, so the words after it fall apart and are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wagner's opera Twilight of the Gods was not really written by the composer credited.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics invoke Götterdämmerung, Wagner's opera, but only 'Downfall of' is the anagram signal acting on 'the Gods'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghosted book is written by a hidden ghostwriter, so the named author did not actually write it.

clue.text: One put in charge of collection, as clergyman virtually gets nothing right

definitions.text: One put in charge of collection

indicators.note: virtually means almost, so the word falls just short of complete

parts.note: a curate is an assistant parish priest
O looks like zero
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A vicar is appointed to oversee the church collection plate and ends up with no money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collection' suggests the church offering, but the definition is a museum keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A curator is the person who looks after a museum or gallery's collection of objects.

clue.text: To recover, it needs a sort of miracle

indicators.note: a sort of means a variety, so the letters take a different form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Getting it back would take something close to a miracle.
explanation.definitionFit: To reclaim something is to get it back after losing it, which is to recover it.

clue.text: Criticise one answer that could fix everything

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun: something that could fix everything

parts.note: to pan a play is to criticise it harshly
an ace is the one in a pack of cards
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Someone attacks a proposed solution claimed to cure every problem.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea is a supposed universal remedy, a cure for all ills or difficulties.

clue.text: Cut out Scotch if another drink's provided

parts.note: to pink is to cut a zigzag edge in cloth, as with pinking shears
gin is a Scots dialect word meaning if

explanation.surface: Stop serving whisky if some other drink is laid on.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotch looks like whisky, or the verb put a stop to; it says the next word is in Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Pink gin is a cocktail of gin flavoured with Angostura bitters, a different tipple from Scotch.

clue.text: Listen to hard rock

indicators.note: listening means we attend to how the word sounds, not how it is spelt

parts.note: tough means hard

explanation.surface: An order to hear some heavy rock music.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard rock looks like a music genre; the definition is the single word 'rock'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuff is a porous volcanic stone formed from compacted ash, so it is a type of rock.

clue.text: Quick read is inadequate — no conclusion reached

indicators.note: with no conclusion the word loses its ending

parts.note: scant means insufficient

explanation.surface: A skim through a report is too thin to reach any verdict.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan a page is to glance over it rapidly, so a scan is a hurried look through text.

clue.text: In US, refuse to reelect any seriously hated leaders

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: American voters decline to re-elect deeply unpopular politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as the verb decline; it is the noun meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Trash is the everyday American word for household rubbish, which the British call refuse.

clue.text: Very musical fool? Excellent!

definitions.note: musical marks the field: very, as a musical direction

parts.note: an ass is a fool
A1 means first-rate, with the 1 written as I

explanation.surface: A very musical idiot gets a cry of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: Assai is Italian for very, as in allegro assai, very fast.
explanation.definitionFit: In musical tempo directions assai is the Italian intensifier, so it is the musicians' word for very.

clue.text: Place fills completely?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: what satisfies entirely is said to hit this, as a good meal does

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the looser second sense: food that fills you completely 'hits the spot'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot is a particular place, and the idiom 'hits the spot' describes something wholly satisfying.

clue.text: Deck reshuffled at the start in return game

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the word is read in the opposite direction
in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: polo is a game played on horseback

indicators.note: at the start points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of reshuffled

explanation.surface: A pack of cards is shuffled before a rematch begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' suggests cards, given 'reshuffled', but it is a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: The orlop is the lowest deck of a sailing ship, below the waterline.

clue.text: One attacking king in time, thus, with rook

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the other

parts.note: ages means a long time
GR, Georgius Rex, is King George
so means in this way
R is the chess abbreviation for rook

explanation.surface: A chess move: a player attacks the king in good time, using the rook.
explanation.walkthrough: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George, as on British post boxes.
explanation.definitionFit: An aggressor is the party who starts a fight or launches an assault on another.

clue.text: A more impotent version of sick European chap?

definitions.note: plays on the historical label 'the sick man of Europe'

indicators.note: a version is a different rendering, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An ailing man from Europe is described as rather less potent.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nineteenth century the declining Turkish state was nicknamed 'the sick man of Europe'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsar Nicholas I called the failing Turkish realm the sick man of Europe, a historical nickname.
